“Just debates about their religion and some guy named Jesus who died—but Paul says He’s alive.”
“I was stuck, so I asked if Paul wanted to go to Jerusalem for trial.”
“But he appealed to Caesar, so I’m holding him till I can send him to Rome.”
Agrippa said, “I wanna hear this guy myself.” Festus said, “You’ll hear him tomorrow.”
The next day, Agrippa and Bernice rolled in with full royal drip—big entrance into the audience hall with top officials.
Festus said, “King Agrippa and crew, here’s the man all the Jews are screaming about.”
“I found nothing death-worthy, but he appealed to Caesar, so I’m sending him.”
“But I’ve got nothing solid to write to the emperor. That’s awkward.”
“So I brought him here—especially for you, King Agrippa—so we can figure out what to say.”
Agrippa said, “You may speak.” So Paul stretched out his hand and started his defense.
“King Agrippa, I’m hyped to defend myself today—especially since you know Jewish customs and beef.”
“So please hear me out with patience.”
“Everyone knows my backstory—I grew up in Jerusalem, living the strict Pharisee life.”
“They’ve known me forever. If they’re honest, they’ll admit I was the most extra Pharisee in the room.”
“Now I’m on trial for believing in the promise God made to our ancestors.”
“The same promise our twelve tribes hope for, serving God day and night.”
“Why’s it wild to believe God raises the dead?”
“I used to think I had to shut down the name of Jesus of Nazareth.”
“I did just that in Jerusalem—locked up believers, voted for executions, hunted them in other cities.”
“I even tried to make them blaspheme—full-on rage mode.”
“Then one day, on my way to Damascus with authority papers…”
“…around noon, I saw a light from heaven—brighter than the sun—blasting around me and my squad.”
“We all hit the ground. I heard a voice in Hebrew: ‘Saul, Saul, why you coming for Me? It’s hard to fight the One you’re kicking against.’”
“I said, ‘Who are You, Lord?’ He said, ‘I’m Jesus—the One you’re dragging.’”
“‘Get up. I’m choosing you to be My witness—to show and tell what you’ve seen and what’s coming.’”
“‘I’m sending you to the Gentiles to open their eyes, turn them from darkness to light, from Satan to God.’”
“‘They’ll get forgiveness and a place in My fam by faith.’”
“So, King Agrippa, I didn’t ghost the vision—I went all in.”
“I told people everywhere—repent, turn to God, and live it out.”
“That’s why the Jews grabbed me in the temple and tried to kill me.”
“But God’s had my back. I’m still here, testifying to everyone—saying nothing new, just what Moses and the prophets said.”
“That the Messiah would suffer, rise from the dead, and bring light to Jews and Gentiles.”
Festus shouted, “Paul, you’ve lost it! Too much studying fried your brain!”
Paul said, “I’m not crazy, most excellent Festus. I’m speaking facts—sober and true.”
“The king knows what I’m saying. I’m speaking boldly because none of this was done in secret.”
“King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.”
Agrippa said, “You really think you can make me a Christian that quick?”
Paul said, “Quick or slow—I wish everyone listening would be like me… except for these chains.”
The king, governor, Bernice, and the squad stood up.
As they left, they said, “This guy hasn’t done anything worth death or prison.”
Agrippa told Festus, “He could’ve been set free… if he hadn’t appealed to Caesar.”
When it was decided we’d sail to Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius from the Imperial Squad.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was headed to ports along the coast of Asia, and set sail. Aristarchus, a bro from Thessalonica, rolled with us.
The next day we docked at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and let him visit his friends to get supplies.
From there we sailed out, but the winds were against us, so we hugged the coast of Cyprus.
We crossed the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, then landed at Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship headed for Italy and put us on board.
We made slow progress for many days and barely reached Cnidus. The wind kept blocking us, so we sailed under Crete, near Salmone.
We struggled along the coast and came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
A lot of time had passed, and sailing was now dangerous since the Day of Atonement had passed. Paul gave them a warning:
“Guys, I see this trip ending in disaster—not just cargo and ship, but lives too.”
But the centurion listened more to the pilot and ship owner than to Paul.
Since the harbor wasn’t great for wintering, most voted to sail on to Phoenix, hoping to winter there.
When a gentle south wind blew, they thought they had it. They pulled anchor and hugged the coast of Crete.
But soon a violent wind called the Northeaster slammed down from the island.
The ship got caught and couldn’t face the wind, so we gave up and let it drive us.
We passed under a small island called Clauda and barely secured the lifeboat.
The crew hoisted it up, tied ropes under the ship to hold it together, and lowered the sea anchor, afraid of running aground on the sandbars of Syrtis.
The storm kept raging, so the next day they started tossing cargo overboard.
On the third day, they threw the ship’s gear overboard with their own hands.
The sun and stars disappeared for days. The storm raged on. We gave up all hope of surviving.
After they hadn’t eaten in a while, Paul stood up and said, “You should’ve listened to me and stayed in Crete. Could’ve avoided all this.”
“But now I urge you—don’t lose hope. Not one of you will die. Only the ship’s going down.”
“Last night, an angel from the God I serve stood by me and said,”
“Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar. God’s got you—and everyone sailing with you.”
“So take heart, fam. I believe God. It’ll go down just like He said.”
“But we’re gonna crash on some island.”
On the fourteenth night, we were still drifting in the Adriatic Sea when the crew sensed we were nearing land.
They dropped a line and found the water was 20 fathoms deep. A bit later, 15.
Afraid we’d hit rocks, they dropped four anchors from the back and prayed for daylight.
Some sailors tried to bail, pretending to lower anchors while actually dropping the lifeboat.
Paul told the centurion and soldiers, “If they leave, we’re all done for.”
So the soldiers cut the ropes and let the lifeboat drift away.
Just before dawn, Paul urged everyone to eat: “You’ve gone 14 days without food. You need strength to survive.”
“Not a hair on your heads will be lost. Trust me.”
He took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and started eating.
Everyone felt encouraged and ate too.
There were 276 of us on board.
After eating, they lightened the ship by tossing the grain into the sea.
When daylight came, they didn’t recognize the land but saw a bay with a beach and aimed to run the ship ashore.
They cut the anchors loose, untied the rudders, hoisted the foresail, and made for the beach.
But they hit a sandbar and ran aground. The front stuck fast, and the back started breaking apart in the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none could escape.
But the centurion wanted to save Paul, so he stopped them. He ordered those who could swim to jump first and head for land.
The rest followed on planks or debris. And just like Paul said—everyone made it out alive.
After we made it to shore, we found out the island was called Malta.
The locals were super kind—they built a fire and welcomed us, even though it was raining and freezing.
Paul gathered some sticks, and when he threw them on the fire, a viper jumped out from the heat and latched onto his hand.
The locals saw the snake hanging and said, “This guy must be cursed—he escaped the sea, but justice won’t let him live.”
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire like it was nothing and didn’t even flinch.
They waited for him to swell up or drop dead—but after a while, when nothing happened, they flipped and said, “He’s a god!”
Nearby was land owned by a chief named Publius. He welcomed us and let us stay for three days.
His dad was sick in bed with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed, laid hands on him, and healed him.
After that, all the sick people on the island came through—and got healed too.
The people honored us big time and loaded us with supplies when we were ready to sail.
After three months, we boarded an Alexandrian ship with twin gods as its figurehead, wintered at the island.
We stopped at Syracuse and stayed three days.
From there we sailed to Rhegium. A day later, a south wind kicked in, and we reached Puteoli the next day.
We found some believers there who invited us to stay a week. Then we headed to Rome.
The believers there heard we were coming and met us at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and felt strengthened.
When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself—with a soldier guarding him.
Three days later, Paul called the Jewish leaders together and said, “Brothers, I’ve done nothing against our people or traditions, yet I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed to the Romans.”
“They examined me and wanted to let me go—no death sentence on me.”
“But the Jews objected, so I had to appeal to Caesar—not that I had anything against my own people.”
“That’s why I asked to see you and talk. I’m in these chains because of the hope of Israel.”
They replied, “We haven’t gotten any letters about you, and no one’s said anything bad. But we want to hear your side.”
“This sect you’re part of—we’ve heard people everywhere talking against it.”
So they set a day, and a crowd came to Paul’s place. From morning to night, he explained the kingdom of God and tried to convince them about Jesus from the Law and the Prophets.
Some were convinced. Others weren’t buying it.
They couldn’t agree and started leaving. But Paul dropped one last word: “The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke through Isaiah to your ancestors,
saying, ‘Go to this people and say: You’ll hear but not get it. You’ll see but not perceive.’
‘Their hearts are hard. Ears plugged. Eyes shut. Otherwise they’d turn and be healed.’”
“So just know—this salvation from God has been sent to the nations. And they’re actually listening.”
And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves.
Paul stayed two whole years in his rented spot. He welcomed everyone who came through,
preaching the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ—with full boldness, no one stopping him.
